title: Amazon Lambda Pricing: Cost Breakdown for 2026
summary: Amazon Lambda pricing includes charges for requests, execution time, and optional features. Your costs depend on function frequency and execution duration.
body_markdown:
## Frequently asked questions


### Is AWS Lambda free?


Not beyond a monthly allowance, and that allowance covers only Lambda's own requests and compute time.


Historically it hasn't expired after the first year the way many AWS free tiers do, but AWS has changed free-tier terms for newer accounts, so confirm what your account actually gets.


Elsewhere the trap is bigger: API Gateway, log ingestion, data transfer and NAT gateways are billed separately, and at scale they often outweigh the function itself.


Treat the allowance as a way to run a prototype for nothing, not as a reason to skip the model.


### Does Lambda charge for failed invocations?


Yes, if the function actually ran. You pay for the duration up to the failure, and a timeout bills for the full configured limit, so a generous timeout on a hanging dependency is an expensive mistake. Throttled requests that never start aren't billed as executions.


Retries are the quiet multiplier: asynchronous invocations and event-source retries each run again and each bill again. A poison message that fails repeatedly can cost real money before anyone notices. Set sensible timeouts, cap retries, and route repeated failures to a dead-letter queue.


### How do I estimate my Lambda bill before launch?


Multiply expected monthly requests by average duration and by memory in gigabytes, then add the request charge, and price every service in the request path alongside it.


Pull duration and memory from a load test, not a guess, because duration shifts with memory and a larger allocation sometimes finishes fast enough to cost less.


Include peak concurrency, since your account's concurrency limit decides whether traffic gets throttled before cost becomes the problem.


If you're considering a Savings Plan, model the baseline you'd commit to separately. It's a discount on committed spend, so it rewards steady load and does little for spiky workloads.


Check the current pricing page on the day you run the numbers, because rates and plan terms change.


### Is Arm cheaper than x86 on Lambda?


Usually, on paper: Arm functions are billed at a lower rate per unit of compute time, and many workloads run as fast or faster there. The rate only matters if duration holds, so benchmark both architectures with your real code.


Build native dependencies, compiled extensions and container images for arm64 first, because a package without an Arm build can cost more in migration effort than it saves.


Switch one function, compare billed duration under identical load, and expand only when the measurement agrees with the rate card.
